full_judgment:
SM Maniruzzaman J : Common questions of law and facts are involved in both the writ petitions and have been taken up for hearing together and are being disposed of by this single judgment.

2. These Rules Nisi, issued under Article 102 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, the respondents have been called upon to show cause as to why the impugned order dated 5-1-2006 and 17-4-2006 respectively passed by the respondent No. 1 vide Letter No. ৫ম/২০(১৮)এলসি(এডমিন)/২০০২ (পার্ট-১)/১৯৭২-৯৫ ordering the respondent No. 2 for imposing minimum value at US$ 580 per MT of imported frozen "Hilsha Fish" (Annxure-G & G-1) and assessment order dated 13-7-2006 passed by the respondent No. 4 in Bill of Entry Nos. C-1500-06 and 1499-06 both dated 13-7-2006 imposing minimum value at US$ 580 Per MT of imported frozen "Hilsha Fish" in place of Invoice Value US$ 300 per MT (Annexure-F) should not be declared to have been made without lawful authority and is of no legal effect and/or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

3. At the time of issuance of the Rules, the respondents were directed to release the petitioners' imported consignment under Bill of Entry Nos. C-1500-06 and C-1499-06 both dated 13-7-2006 on payment of customs duties and other taxes on the basis of invoice value and for the difference between the invoice value and the value demanded by the Customs Authority 20% should be paid in cash and on furnishing bank guarantee for the rest within 5 (five) days from the date of receipt of this order. 4. Facts, necessary for disposal of the Rules, in short, are that the petitioners of both the writ petitions are businessman engaged in the business of importation of various home consumption items from abroad and after importation, they sell the same in the local market. Both the petitioners have been continuing their business by obtaining necessary permission from the government concerned.

5. The petitioners in course of their business decided to import 33.333 Metric Ton of frozen "Hilsha Fish" bearing HS Code No. 0303.29.29 from Myanmar. As per the business practice prevalent in Teknaf, the petitioners made Foreign Demand Draft being No. BTA/ FD0005978 dated 117.2006 for an amount of US$ 10,000 and BTA/FD0005998 dated 13-7-2006 for an amount of US$ 10,000 in Sonali Bank, Teknaf Branch, Cox's Bazar in favour of Mayanmar Economic Bank, Maungdaw Branch, Maungdaw, Mayanmar under Border Trade Agreement executed between Myanmar and Bangladesh on 18-5-1994.

6. After receiving the aforesaid payment orders, the supplier made shipment of the goods and issued necessary shipping documents namely Commercial Invoice and Packing List in support of shipment. After arrival of the goods at Land Customs Station, Teknaf, the petitioners of the respective writ petitions submitted Bill of Entry Nos. C-1500-06 and C-1499-06 both dated 13-7-2006 through their C & F agent along with necessary shipping documents for assessment and releasing the consignment on the basis of invoice value. The Customs authority rejected the invoice value at the rate of US$ 300 Per Metric Ton and assessed the goods at the rate of US$ 580 Per Metric Ton being minimum assessable value, which was fixed as per recommendation of the Value Fixation Committee, Customs House, Chattogram. The respondent No.1, the Commissioner, Customs, Excise and VAT Commissionerate, Chattogram had fixed the minimum assessable value of the frozen "Hilsha Fish" at the rate of US$ 580 Per Metric Ton vide letter No. ৫ম/২০(১৮)এলসি(এডমিন)/২০০২ (পার্ট-১)/১২৭-২৯  dated 5-1-2006. Said order came in force on 31-12-2005 and would remain in force till further order (Annexure-G). Subsequent, thereto the said respondent issued another order vide Nothi No. ৫ম/২০(১৮)এলসি(এডমিন)/২০০২ (পার্ট-১)/১৯৭২-৯৫ dated 17-4-2006 fixing the minimum value of some imported goods including the frozen "Hilsha Fish" at the rate of US$ 580 Per Metric Ton giving effect from 16-4-2006 to 30-6-2006 (Annexure-G1).

7. In the supplementary affidavit to the writ petition, it has been further stated that the respondent No.1 by his office order dated 19-7-2006 further fixed minimum value of some imported goods including the frozen "Hilsha Fish" at the rate of US$ 580 per Metric Ton giving effect from 1-7-2006 to 30-9-2006 (Annexure-I). The aforesaid 3 (three) orders were issued by the respondent No.1, fixing the minimum assessable value of frozen "Hilsha Fish" at the rate of US$ 580 per Metric Ton. On the basis of the said minimum value, the respondents Customs authorities have assessed the petitioners' consignment fixing the value of Taka 13,90,207 instead of invoice value of Taka 6,98,000.

8. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the aforesaid office circulars and subsequent assessment orders the petitioners have filed the instant application under Article 102 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh and obtained the present Rules and interim order of stay.

9. Mr MA Hannan, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner in both the writ petitions submits that under the provision of section 25(3) of the Customs Act, 1969 the government has authority to fix minimum value by publishing notification in the official gazette but, no gazette notification was made fixing the minimum value of the frozen "Hilsha Fish" in question under section 25(3) of the said Act. Hence, the fixation of minimum value by the impugned orders are liable to be declared to have been passed without lawful authority. He further goes to submit that there is no existence of the Value Determination Committee either under the Customs Act, 1969 or the Customs Valuation Rules, 2000 and as such, fixation of the value by the Value Determination Committee for the imported frozen "Hilsha Fish" at the rate of US$ 580 Per Metric Ton and on the basis of the said value making assessment of the petitioners' goods in question is fully without jurisdiction. Lastly, he goes to submit that the transaction value of the consignment at the rate of US$ 300 Per Metric Ton has been rejected by the Customs authority and has imposed the value of US$ 580 Per Metric Ton in violation of the provision of rule 3 read with rules 4,5,6,7,8 and 9 of the Valuation Rules, 2000. In support of his contention the learned Advocate for the petitioner has placed reliance on an unreported decision passed by this Court in writ petition No. 2025 of 2006 along with two other writ petitions.

10. Countering the said submissions, Mr Samarendra Nath Biswas, the learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing on behalf of the respondent-government without filing any affidavit-in-opposition, submits that the present Rules must fail as being not maintainable, for the petitioner had alternative forum under the Customs Act, 1969 as well as Customs Valuation Rules, 2000 against the impugned assessment order before the Appellant authority concern, so have been challenged in this writ petition. Hence, the present Rules are liable to be discharged as being not maintainable.

11. We have heard the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner, the learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing for the respondent government, have perused the writ petitions along with annexures so have been appended thereto and relevant provision of the law.

12. Admittedly, the petitioners of the respective writ petitions imported 33.333 Metric Ton frozen "Hilsha Fish" from Myanmar at the rate of US$ 300 Per Metric Ton and total value of the consignment was US$ 10,000. After arrival of the goods at Land Customs Station, Teknaf, Cox's Bazar, the petitioners of respective writ petitions through their C & F agent submitted Bill of Entry Nos. C-1500.06 and C-1499-06 both dated 13-7-2006 for assessment and releasing the goods. On perusal of Bills of Entry (Annexure-F to the writ petitions) it appears that the goods were duly inspected by the Customs authority and found that—

“১০% দৈবচরনের ভিত্তিতে কায়িক করে প্রতি বস্তার গড় নীট ওজন ১৮.৩৯৫৬ কেজি করে পাওয়া যায়। Invoice ও packing list এর ঘোষণা অনুযায়ী মিল রয়েছে।”

13. It also appears that the invoice value of the consignment is US$ 300 Per Metric Ton total invoice value is US$ 10,000 equivalent to Taka 6,98,000 but, the Customs authority without accepting the transaction value has fixed the assessable value of Taka 13,90,207 upon giving adjustment US$ 1.9917% on the invoice value. In this regard, the categorical assertion of the petitioners are that the Customs authority has fixed the assessable value as per direction so given by the respondent No. 1 by his office orders dated 5-1-2006, 17-4-2006 and 19-7-2006 respectively.

14. The cardinal issue requires determination in the instant Rules is that whether the respondent No. 1, the Commissioner, Customs, Excise and VAT is empowered to fix the minimum assessable value of any imported goods as well as frozen "Hilsha Fish" in question by his office order or by recommendation of any committee under the Customs Act, 1969 or Rules framed thereunder. In this regard the learned Advocate for the petitioners has argued that the government is only the authority to frame Rules for determination of assessable value of imported goods and to fix tariff or minimum value of any imported goods by publishing the Gazette notification as per provision under section 25 of the Customs Act. Section 25 of the Customs Act is quoted below:—

"Secion-25: Value of goods for assessment purpose 1. whenever customs duty is leviable on any goods by reference to their value, the actual price, that is, the price actually paid or payable, or the nearest ascertainable equivalent of such price, at which such or like goods are ordinarily sold, or offered for sale, for delivery at the time and place of importation or exportation, as the case may be, in course of international trade under fully competitive conditions, where the seller and the buyer have no interest in the business of each other and the price is the sole consideration for sale or offer for sale, shall be the value.]"

[Explanation—For the purposes of this sub-section, the expression—

[(a) "the time of importation" means the date on which a bill of entry is delivered under section 79.]

(b) "the time of exportation" means the time when the bill of export is delivered under section 131, or, when export of the goods is allowed [under that section] without a bill of export or in anticipation of the presentation of a bill of export, the time when the goods is [?] taken to the customs port or customs airport or customs station for the purpose of export;

(C) (i) "the place of importation" means the customs port or customs airport[?] or the customs station at which the bill of entry is first submitted; and

(ii) "place of exportation"[?] means the customs port or the station[?] at which the bill of export is submitted.]

(2) Subject to the provisions of sub-section (1), the price referred to in that sub-section in respect of imported goods shall be determined in accordance with the rules made in this behalf.

(3) Notwithstanding anything contained in this section, the Government may, by notification in the official Gazette, fix, for the purpose of levying customs duties, tariff values [or minimum values] for any goods imported or exported as chargeable with customs duty ad valorem:

Provided that any imported or exported goods, the declared value of which is higher than its tariff value fixed under this sub-section, shall be chargeable with customs duties on the basis of its declared value.

15. On perusal of the aforesaid section 25, it appears that the government is only the authority to frame Rules for determination of assessable value of imported goods as per sub-section 2 and to fix tariff or minimum value of any imported goods by publishing the notification in the official Gazette as per sub section 3 of section 25 of the Customs Act for the purpose of assessment of the imported goods.

16. In the impugned office orders dated 5-1-2006 (Annexure-G) dated 17-4-2006 (Annexure-G 1) and subsequent order dated 19-7-2006 (Annexure-I) respectively, it appears that the respondent No. 1, the Commissioner, Customs, Excise and VAT had fixed the minimum value of the imported frozen "Hilsha Fish" by those office orders. But, section 25 of the Customs Act has not empowered the Customs authority as well as the respondent No.1 the Commissioner, Custom, Excise and VAT to issue such kind of circulars fixing minimum value of any imported goods. Rather, sub-section (3) of section 25 authorizes only the Government to fix the tariff/minimum value of any imported goods to be determined and fixed by the Gazette notification.

17. In the present case, the respondent No. 1, the Commissioner, Customs, Excise and VAT Commissionerate had fixed the minimum value of some imported goods including the frozen "Hilsha Fish" in question bearing HS Code No. 0303.10.10 at the rate of US$ 580 Per Metric Ton by the impugned office order/ circulars dated 5-1-2006 (Annexure-G) giving effect from 31-12-2005 until further order, Orders dated 17-4-2006 (Annexure-G1) and dated 19-7-2006 (Annexure-I) respectively were circulated by the said respondent giving effect from 16-4-2006 to 30-6-2006 and 1-7-2006 to 30-9-2006 respectively. The petitioner of the respective writ petitions submitted Bill of Entry on 13-7-2006 (Annexure-F to the respective writ petitions) and that the Customs authority had assessed the imported frozen "Hilsha Fish" at the rate of US$ 580 Per Metric Ton on the basis of impugned circulars, not by following the Customs Valuation Rules, 2000.

18. Under the statutory obligation, a government is bound to declare tariff value or minimum value in the official gazette for the purpose of import and export. In the present case, no such gazette notification has been published in respect of importation of frozen "Hilsha Fish" The value as fixed at the rate of US$ 580 Per Metric Ton by the Commissioner, customs, Excise and VAT Commissionerate does not have any sanction of law; rather the same having been issued in violation of section 25(3) of the Customs Act, 1969, it is liable to be knocked down.

19. In this regard, in the unreported case of SM Abdul Alim vs Commissioner of Customs, Customs House, Chittagong and other passed by one of the Benches of this Division in writ petition No. 2025 of 2006, it has been observed, inter-alia that;

"It appears that the respondents get the consignment assessed on the recommendation of the assessment committee which is also illegal and without lawful authority because law does not provide for such mechanism for making the assessment."

20. Also, in the case of Collector of Customs vs TK Oil Refinery Ltd, and 22 others reported in 62 DLR (AD) 217, it has been held that;—

"As it appears, that High Court Division made the Rules absolute holding that a reading Of the provisions of section 25(1)(2)(3) and section 30(1) of the Customs Act show that the Customs Authority is authorised to assess customs duties of imported goods at the value prevalent on the date when the bill of entry is presented for assessment of customs duties but, in the present case, the Customs authority fixed the indicative value for the purpose of assessment of customs duties of the imported CDSO and CPO imported by the respondents long before the presentation of the bill of entry and accordingly, "indicative value, that has been Ned by the circular dated 3-7-94, cannot be considered to have been fixed in the light of the provisions of section 25(1)(2) and (3) of the Customs Act and that in terms of the above section the Customs Authority, in appropriate cases, no doubt, is competent to fix normal value of imported goods upon rejection of the invoice value or the declared value but in such case the Customs authority would be required to notify importers informing them that the Customs authority is not accepting the invoice value or declared value as the basis for the purpose of assessment of customs duty and is going to fix the normal price of the imported goods for the assessment of customs duties and the customs authority would also be required to afford an opportunity to the importers to place their cases, if any, in support of their claim that the invoice value, in fact, is the normal price of the imported merchandise for the purpose of assessment of customs duties or that as against the invoice/declared value of the imported goods the customs authority is going to tax the normal price of the goods for the purpose of assessment of customs duties but, in the instant case, that has not been done by the customs authority and the Customs  authority fixed through internal circular, certain prices of CDSO and CPO for the purpose of assessment of customs duties  terming the same as "indicative value" but  under the Customs Act. the revenue realizing Authority or the Customs Authority is authorised to fix tariff value under 'section 25(7) of the Act at a prior date through Gazette notification for the purpose of assessment of customs duties and the  indicative value that has been fixed later On and circulated through Circular dated 3-7-94  was admittedly not notified in the official Gazette,"

21. Further, it has been held that;—

"As it appears, at the conclusion, that High Court Division directed that the customs authority is to assess the customs duties of the goods in respect of which the letters of credit were opened prior to the deletion of the tariff value by the SRO dated 9-6-1994 on the basis of tariff value prevalent at the time of opening of letters of credit and in other cases taking the invoice value but the above order of the High Court Division to the extent that "in other cases taking the invoice value" is modified to the extent, that if the invoice  value as shown by the respondents are not acceptable to them the Customs Authority  will be at liberty to fix normal price in terms  of the provisions of section 25(1) of the  Customs Act is accordance with law and then assess customs duty and other duties on the  basis of normal price so fixed."

22. In view of the above, fixing the value of frozen "Hilsha Fish" by the Commissioner, Customs, Excise and VAT, Commissionerate, Chattogram in the impugned official circulars has no legal basis and without sanction of law.

<u>23. The assertion of the learned Deputy Attorney-General in respect of availability of the alternative remedy, in the present context is a misconceived one, it is the settled principle of law that when an illegality is apparent on the face of record and the respondents performing the function of the Republic have acted totally without jurisdiction, invoking forum as provided under Article 102 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh is not a bar. The fiAtion of minimum value by the respondent No. 1, the Commissioner of Customs, Excise and VAT, Chattogram without publishing in the Gazette notification ,and assessment thereafter pursuant to the said ,value is without jurisdiction.</u>

24. In view of the above, the forum as provided under the Customs Act, 1969 is not a bar invoking Special Original Jurisdiction as provided under Article 102 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh.

25. Considering the facts and circumstances of the cases as stated hereinabove, we find substance to the contention so have been raised by the petitioners and accordingly we are inclined to make the Rules absolute.

26. In the result, both the Rules are made absolute without any order as to cost. The fixation of the minimum value of Frozen "Hilsha Fish" under HS Code No. 0303.39.10 at rate of US$ 580 Per Metric Ton by the official circulars dated 5-1-2006, 17-4-2006 and 19-7-2006 (Annexure-G, G1, I respectively), pursuant thereto the assessment order as appeared in Bill of Entry Nos. C-1500-06 and 1499-06 both dated 13-7-2006 (Annexure-F to the writ petitions) are hereby declared to have been passed without jurisdiction and hence, of no legal effect.

27. Since, the goods in question have already been released by the Customs authority on the basis of interim order of direction so passed by this Court at the time of issuance of the Rules, in this situation, the concerned respondent is hereby directed to assess finally the imported goods of the petitioners, covered under Bill of Entry Nos. C-1500-06 and 1499-06 both dated 13-7-2006 fixing the normal value under the provision of the Customs Valuation Rules, 2000 and shall return back the bank guarantee if the amount (if any) that becomes due after such final assessment is paid in cash within 120 (one hundred twenty) day from the date of receipt of the copy of this judgment and order, positively.

Communicate the copy of the judgment and order to the concerned respondents forthwith.

End.
